---
title: "Using R"
---

This book relies on the reader using R for both analyses and reporting. You can learn more about R and stay on top of recent developments by following <https://www.r-project.org/>. There are many introductory resources available for using R as an analytical tool. This book will take care of the "reporting" component with R. 

The expectation is that you are familiar with three important R "components": 

1. an interactive console
2. a scripting environment
3. helper packages

@fig-renviron presents two components, the console and a script file. The script file has two elementary elements within it: 1) a comment line (identified by at least one octothorpe^[Kulas prefers two octothorpes as a commenting convention -- this is merely personal preference, but it will be repeatedly encountered throughout this book]), and 2) a command (`2 + 2`). The manner in which you access R is "up to you". Many Psychology students like the R Studio interface (referred to as an "IDE" -- Integrated Development Environment), but many options exist. 

![Screenshot of R console and scripting environment](/img/renviron.JPG){#fig-renviron}

Any additional experience you may have with R is great, but if you understand the 3 critical components (as well as the specification of comments), have a positive attitude about R^[This is not trivial!!! Students who "fail" at R do so because of attitude, not a lack of ability], and follow the copy--paste format of this book, you should be fine.

Throughout this book, we will provide code that you can execute as example analyses -- you can copy code that we provide and paste it into your local R session (and tweak/play with the code to better your own personal understanding of "what is happening").

For example, if you engage the clipboard ({{< iconify bi:clipboard >}}) in @lst-example and paste into your R session (either within a script file or the console), you should return the output `[1] 4`:

```{r}
#| lst-label: lst-example
#| lst-cap: Example bit of code to copy/paste
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

2 + 2

```

The code we share later in the book is a bit more elaborate, but the copy/paste process is the same regardless of how sophisticated the analytical content is (or isn't). 

## Example Measure {#sec-example}

If you follow the recommendations of this book, you will (eventually) produce your own unique measure and administer it to a sample of your choosing. However, before you do that, we will demonstrate Psychometric ***principles and practices*** utilizing a [shared]{.underline} measure and dataset: the `bfi` from within the [`psych` package](https://personality-project.org/r/psych/). 

@sec-example highlights important information about this dataset, primarily:  

1. What are the items?
2. What are the scales?
3. What are the scale definitions?^[what items are associated with what scales, and are any recodes or differential weighting algorithms necessary]
4. What demographics were collected?

The [BFI dataset](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/psych/versions/2.2.3/topics/bfi) (from the `psych` R package) contains 2,800 responses to 28 variables. The 28 variables are presented in @tbl-bfidefs. The 2,800 responses are contained within the `bfi` object and will be used to demonstrate Psychometric analyses.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bfidefs
#| tbl-cap: "Variables of focal interest within the `bfi` data object"
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

bfivars <- psych::bfi.dictionary[,c(2,4,6)]

DT::datatable(bfivars, options = list(pageLength = 5))
      
```

## Using R

For each topic that involves analytical exploration, we will provide template R script that you can  copy--paste into your local R session^[sometimes the script will require "pre--processing" such that previous scripts must first be executed prior to the desired code operating as expected.]. See @lst-tutor1 for an example that:  

1. loads the `psych` package
2. accesses the `bfi` dataset
3. asks for a histogram of age
4. asks for the mean and standard deviation for the age variable

```{r}
#| lst-label: lst-tutor1
#| lst-cap: "WebR code example"
#| echo: true
library(psych)

data(bfi)

hist(bfi$age)

mean(bfi$age)
sd(bfi$age)
```
